_README: Devotional name elements that land in the SURNAME position but do not
Why this file exists: `_surname_of` takes the last token of a name, so
'Maria Josefa de la Concepcion' has the surname 'Concepcion' and 'Juan de la
Cruz' has 'Cruz'. Two unrelated women both recorded 'de la Cruz' therefore
have surnames that match EXACTLY, and an exact match takes the exemption in
surname_tier_allows -- the tiered bars only govern surnames that DIFFER. So
the most-shared names in the corpus were the ones with the least scrutiny.
Measured before the fix: 63 merged identities rested on an epithet, holding
699 mentions, every large one spanning multiple volumes.
What listing a term here does: it does NOT block the merge and does NOT
change the stored name. It only removes the exact-match shortcut, so the pair
must clear the same corroboration bar a near-variant spelling does (shared
register, people named in both entries, close dates, agreeing attributes).
A genuine Cruz family usually clears it easily; two strangers who happen to
share a Marian epithet usually do not.
`ambiguous` terms are ones that are also ordinary inherited surnames. They
are treated the same way, but listed separately because they are the ones

ambiguous.cruz: Both a Marian epithet ('de la Cruz') and one of the commonest inherited Hispanic surnames. 28 of the 63 affected identities hang off this one term.
ambiguous.flores: 'de las Flores' is devotional; Flores is also an ordinary surname.
ambiguous.caridad: 'de la Caridad' (Caridad del Cobre) is devotional in Cuban registers; also used as a given name.
ambiguous.santos: 'dos Santos' is extremely common in Portuguese registers as an inherited surname, not only devotional.
ambiguous.reyes: 'de los Reyes' (Epiphany) is devotional; Reyes is also inherited.
ambiguous.salvador: Devotional, and also a given name and a surname.
